nameStory: The name 'wigeon' comes from the French word 'vigeon,' which itself derives from the Latin 'vipio' meaning a type of small crane. The musical whistling calls these ducks make likely inspired the melodic-sounding name. European settlers brought the name with them, and it stuck for both the European species and its American cousin.
description: The Eurasian Wigeon is a medium-sized dabbling duck that's an uncommon but regular visitor to New England from Europe and Asia. Males in breeding plumage sport a striking rusty-red head with a creamy yellow stripe running from the forehead to the back of the head, earning them the nickname 'redhead' among birders. Females are more subdued with warm brown plumage and a rounded head profile. These compact ducks are slightly smaller than a Mallard, with a distinctive steep forehead and relatively small bill.

idTips.label: Male's cream forehead stripe
idTips.description: Breeding males show a distinctive pale yellow or cream-colored stripe running from the bill base over the crown - this bold racing stripe contrasts beautifully against the rusty-red head

idTips.label: Steep forehead profile
idTips.description: The head has a distinctly rounded, steep forehead that drops sharply to a small grayish bill - gives the bird an almost bullet-headed appearance when seen in profile

idTips.label: White wing patches
idTips.description: In flight, both sexes flash prominent white patches on the upper wings that appear as bright rectangular windows - these are easily visible even at distance

idTips.label: Whistling call notes
idTips.description: Males give a distinctive musical whistle that sounds like 'whee-oo' - much more melodic and pure-toned than the quacks of most other ducks

idTips.label: Compact body size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more compact than Mallards when seen together - the body appears almost chunky with a relatively short neck

habitat: Look for Eurasian Wigeons in shallow freshwater ponds, marshes, and coastal areas throughout New England, especially during migration periods. They prefer areas with abundant aquatic vegetation and often join mixed flocks with American Wigeons and other dabbling ducks. Coastal salt ponds, large inland lakes, and flooded agricultural fields are prime spots to search.

seasonality.spring: Most sightings occur during spring migration from March through May, when males display their brightest breeding plumage with the distinctive cream head stripe most prominent.
seasonality.summer: Very rare in summer, with only occasional non-breeding individuals remaining in the region - most have returned to their Arctic and subarctic breeding grounds.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration brings another chance to spot them from September through November, though males may be in duller eclipse plumage that's harder to distinguish.
seasonality.winter: Uncommon winter residents, particularly along the coast where ice-free water remains available - look for them mixed in with flocks of American Wigeons and other ducks.

funFact: Eurasian Wigeons are such efficient grazers that they can completely strip underwater plants by working as a coordinated team - they'll form feeding lines like tiny aquatic combines, systematically harvesting entire beds of pondweed and leaving nothing but bare mud behind.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the American Wigeon, but male Eurasian Wigeons have a cream or yellow forehead stripe instead of white, and rusty-red (not green) extending behind the eye. Remember: 'Eurasian = rusty head with cream stripe, American = gray head with white cap.'
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of the more exciting finds for New England birders since it's a genuine rarity from across the Atlantic. Most sightings are likely birds that got caught up with American Wigeon flocks during migration and crossed over from western North America, where they're more regular visitors.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the American Wigeon, the Eurasian Wigeon male has a rusty-red head with cream forehead stripe versus the American's gray face with white crown stripe. Female Eurasians tend to have warmer, more rufous-toned plumage overall. The third relative, Gadwall, lacks the prominent white wing patches and has a much more subdued gray and brown appearance with an orange-sided bill.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Gadwalls are much more subdued than their Mareca cousins - American wigeons show bold white crown stripes and green eye patches, while Eurasian wigeons display rusty-red heads.
Compared to its closest relative the Gadwall, American Wigeons have much more contrasting plumage with that bright white belly, while Gadwalls are more uniformly gray-brown.
